title: Work, Energy, and Energy Resources
learning_objectives: Define work as force times displacement along the force, and tell it from everyday usage.
Use the work-energy theorem and the gravitational potential energy to solve problems.
Explain what a conservative force is and how potential energy is defined from it.
Apply conservation of energy, and calculate power.

sections.title: Introduction to Work, Energy, and Energy Resources
objectives: Describe what work means in physics and why energy is a better tool for many problems.

misconceptions.claim: Work and energy are two words for the same thing.
misconceptions.correction: They are not. Work is a transfer of energy by a force through a displacement, and energy is the capacity to do work.

summary: Work measures an energy transfer, and energy measures the capacity to do work.
The energy approach often avoids forces and accelerations entirely.
sections.no_worked_example_reason: The source carries no worked example for this section and no solved exercise to promote, so the practice is left to the exercises themselves.

sections.title: Work: The Scientific Definition
objectives: Compute the work done by a constant force as force times the displacement along the force.

misconceptions.claim: Work is force times the distance the object travelled.
misconceptions.correction: It is force times the component of the displacement along the force. A push at right angles to the motion does no work at all.

summary: W = Fd cos(theta), and the angle is measured from the force to the displacement.
A force perpendicular to the motion does no work.
Work is done on the object, and it changes the object's energy.

sections.title: Kinetic Energy and the Work-Energy Theorem
objectives: Use the work-energy theorem to relate the work done on a body to its change in kinetic energy.

misconceptions.claim: Kinetic energy depends on how heavy the body is.
misconceptions.correction: It depends on the mass and on the square of the speed, so a body twice as fast has four times the kinetic energy.

summary: K = 1/2 mv^2, and the speed enters as a square.
The net work done on a body is the change in its kinetic energy.
Doubling the speed multiplies the kinetic energy by four.

sections.title: Gravitational Potential Energy
objectives: Compute the change in gravitational potential energy as the change in height times the weight.

misconceptions.claim: Potential energy depends on where the object is and on nothing else.
misconceptions.correction: It depends on the height and on the weight of the body, so a heavier body at the same height has more of it.

summary: U = mgh, measured against a chosen zero level.
The change in potential energy is the weight times the change in height.
Only the change matters, so the zero level is a choice, not a fact.

sections.title: Conservative Forces and Potential Energy
objectives: Explain what makes a force conservative and how potential energy is defined from it.

misconceptions.claim: A conservative force does no work around a closed path.
misconceptions.correction: It does zero net work around any closed path, so the work depends only on the endpoints, and a potential energy can be defined.

summary: A conservative force does zero net work around a closed path.
Its potential energy depends on position alone, not on the path.
Gravity and the spring force are conservative; friction is not.

sections.title: Nonconservative Forces
objectives: Explain why a nonconservative force changes the mechanical energy of a system.

misconceptions.claim: Friction does no work, because the force is small.
misconceptions.correction: Friction does work on whatever it acts on, and that work is not recoverable, so the mechanical energy falls.

summary: Friction turns mechanical energy into thermal energy.
The mechanical energy of the system falls by the work friction does.
Drag behaves the same way, and it is why a coasting object slows.

sections.title: Conservation of Energy
objectives: Apply conservation of energy to problems that Newton's laws make hard.

misconceptions.claim: Energy is conserved only when there is no friction.
misconceptions.correction: Total energy is always conserved. What friction changes is how much of it is mechanical.

summary: With no friction, the mechanical energy is constant.
With friction, the mechanical energy falls and the thermal energy rises by the same amount.
Energy is conserved whether or not the mechanical energy is.

sections.title: Power
objectives: Define power as the rate of doing work and relate it to energy and to force times speed.

misconceptions.claim: Power is the amount of work done.
misconceptions.correction: Power is the rate: work done per unit time, so the same work done twice as fast is twice the power.

summary: P = W/t, and in energy units P = dE/dt.
P = Fv for a force along the motion.
Power says how fast energy is transferred, not how much.

caption.text: Work done by a constant force

conditions.text: For a constant force, with the angle measured between the force and the displacement.
For a body of mass m moving at speed v.
Measured against a chosen zero level, with h the height above it.
The net work done on a body is the change in its kinetic energy.
The rate of doing work, or of transferring energy.

caption.text: Power from a force and a speed

conditions.text: For a force along the direction of motion.

definition.text: The energy transferred by a force through a displacement, equal to the component of the force along the displacement times the displacement.
The energy a body has because it is moving, equal to half its mass times the square of its speed.
Energy a body has because of its position or its condition, such as its height or the compression of a spring.
A force whose work depends only on the endpoints of the motion, so it does zero net work around a closed path.
The sum of the kinetic and the potential energy of a system.
The rate at which work is done or energy is transferred.

exam_traps.misconception: A conservative force does positive work around a closed path, because the path is longer.
exam_traps.correction: It does zero net work around any closed path, which is what makes a potential energy possible.

exam_traps.correction: Friction does not destroy energy. It turns mechanical energy into thermal energy, so the total energy is unchanged.

exam_traps.misconception: In the power formula the mass is used instead of the weight.

exam_recall_checks.subject: physics
exam_recall_checks.stem: A force of 10 N acts at 60 degrees to the direction of the motion, over a distance of 4 m. How much work is done?
exam_recall_checks.explanation: Work is force times the displacement along the force, so W = 10 x 4 x cos 60 = 20 J.
exam_recall_checks.source: authored against the JAMB physics syllabus

exam_recall_checks.subject: physics
exam_recall_checks.stem: A body of mass 2 kg moves at 6 m/s. What is its kinetic energy?
exam_recall_checks.source: authored against the WAEC physics syllabus

exam_recall_checks.subject: physics
exam_recall_checks.stem: A body of mass 5 kg is lifted through 3 m. What is the gain in gravitational potential energy? (Take g = 10 m/s2.)
exam_recall_checks.explanation: The gain is the weight times the height, so U = mg h = 5 x 10 x 3 = 150 J.
exam_recall_checks.source: authored against the WAEC physics syllabus

exam_recall_checks.subject: physics
exam_recall_checks.stem: A body is moved around a closed path and returns to where it started. For a conservative force the net work done over the path is

options.text: equal to the work done by friction

exam_recall_checks.explanation: A conservative force does zero net work around any closed path, so the work depends only on the endpoints.
exam_recall_checks.source: authored against the WAEC physics syllabus

exam_recall_checks.subject: physics
exam_recall_checks.stem: A block slides down a rough slope and its mechanical energy falls. What has happened to the energy?
exam_recall_checks.explanation: Total energy is conserved. Friction turns the mechanical energy into thermal energy, so the mechanical energy falls by exactly that amount.
exam_recall_checks.source: authored against the JAMB physics syllabus

exam_recall_checks.subject: physics
exam_recall_checks.stem: A machine does 600 J of work in 4 s. What is its power?
exam_recall_checks.explanation: Power is work done per second, so P = 600/4 = 150 W.
exam_recall_checks.source: authored against the JAMB physics syllabus
